Seaver, the family representative who announced Parton's death last month at the age of 80 , received a termination notice September 16 saying that he and his security guard employees had been dismissed, according to TMZ . He served as the head of security for more than two decades after taking over for his father, Larry Seaver, who previously held the role. Footage from last week obtained by TMZ showed replacement guards taking over posts at Parton's home in Nashville, as well as her museum and warehouse. Seaver called out Parton's longtime manager, Danny Nozell, and Pinnacle Bank, who oversees Parton's trust, in a statement to TMZ, saying he and his teams were "dismayed by the unexpected and, so far, unexplained actions." Dolly Parton's nephew Bryan Seaver has reportedly been fired as head of security (Getty Images/Dolly Parton) Nozell did not immediately return The Independent 's request for comment. The termination letter sent to Seaver reportedly states that the DP Dean Trust, which Parton established as her private estate trust before her death, controls Parton's properties and business ventures. The letter clarified that Seaver's personal interest in the trust is unchanged. Seaver and his team said they have been overwhelmed by the love and support shown to Parton's family and her legacy after her death. "We remain unshakably resolved to fulfill her final directive to protect her family," Seaver and his team told TMZ . "And we refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much." The Independent has reached out to Seaver through his company for further comment. The shake-up over Dolly Parton's property security comes nearly a month after her death (AFP/Getty) Parton died August 25 following "a brief battle with cancer" at a hospital in Nashville, where she had been hospitalized four days earlier. The type of cancer has not been disclosed. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," Seaver said at the time. "It is an honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness. But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus." Parton was laid to rest at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville. She was buried next to Carl Dean , her husband of 60 years who died in March 2025. extraction.body: By Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-PedersenCOPENHAGEN, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Denmark, Greenland and the US are to sign a ⁠deal ⁠on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will ⁠put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington and Copenhagen.The agreement, to be signed at the UN ​General Assembly in New York at 10:30 a.m. Denmark and Greenland say the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty.The deal is expected to ‌allow the US, which already has one military base in ‌Greenland, to expand its military presence to two additional sites.One of those sites is Narsarsuaq, whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the US closed its Cold War-era Bluie West One ⁠military base there in ⁠the 1950s. The other is Mestersvig, a military outpost currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a special ​forces unit that enforces Danish sovereignty in the territory, said two people familiar with the matter.Trump will meet in New York on Tuesday with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen for a trilateral signing ceremony, a White House official said. The deal follows months of pressure from Trump, who has said the US should control Greenland and at times refused to rule out using military or economic force to acquire the ​semi-autonomous Danish territory. His threats peaked in January, triggering a diplomatic crisis within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the military defense alliance, and pushing Denmark and Greenland into negotiations ⁠aimed ⁠at defusing the pressure.The agreement "will be in ⁠a form where responsibility for security in ​the Arctic is not only Danish or American," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sunday. He said that to a large extent "it would ​be NATO that looks after the Arctic."BOOSTING NATO'S 'COHESION'It remained unclear ⁠whether the deal amends an existing 1951 defence agreement that is the legal basis for the US presence in Greenland. "It appears that we are now using this crisis to try to strengthen NATO's cohesion through Greenland," said Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS).Washington's strategic interest in Greenland dates back to World War Two. In 1941, the US signed a deal with Danish envoy Henrik Kauffmann, who acted without authority from his country, then under German occupation. The US sought the deal to keep Greenland out of German hands and secure the North Atlantic supply route between North America and Europe. ⁠Under the agreement, the US built airfields, naval facilities, and weather stations across the island, reaching around 5,500 military personnel by 1943, according to ⁠DIIS.In 1946, President Harry Truman sought to buy the island as a strategic asset for $100 million in gold, but Copenhagen declined to sell. Instead, a new agreement was signed in 1951 that gave the US military extensive rights in Greenland but was tied to the existence of NATO."I don't think Denmark and Greenland will sign if the same NATO clause isn't included," said Gad.PROMOTING 'SECURITY, STABILITY AND COOPERATION'During the Cold War, the US maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 US military personnel.A NATO spokesperson said on Saturday that the alliance welcomed the new agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region". Rasmussen, who travelled to New York overnight, declined to discuss the contents of the agreement."But we have said from the start that we are open to accommodating the United States' legitimate security interests," he told Danish news agency Ritzau on Monday.Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Friday the agreement gave the US "permanent control over security, and ⁠all other needs, in Greenland," and that no US adversary could have a base or military presence there without Washington's written approval. Denmark has not responded to Trump's assertion, though Copenhagen earlier acknowledged it underinvested in Greenland's defence for decades and has pledged to expand its military presence on the island, including more NATO troops.Greenland's government has sought to reassure the public about the deal.Erik Jensen, an opposition lawmaker in Greenland, wrote on social media that he had read the draft agreement. "I feel reassured and am not worried," ​he said, adding that the island's foreign minister was handling the work well.(Reporting by Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen in Copenhagen; additional reporting by Steve ​Holland in Washington and Marie Mannes in Stockholm; Editing by Gareth Jones and Rosalba O'Brien)Copyright 2026 Thomson Reuters.

sources.title: US, Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security, Trump says - dw.com
passages: The deal with Denmark, according to President Donald Trump, would give the US "permanent control" over Greenland's security.
Denmark said the deal is "great for NATO and Europe."

"At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump said the US would "immediately" begin expanding its military presence in Greenland.
He added that the agreement recognized "Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation."

extraction.body: The deal with Denmark, according to President Donald Trump, would give the US "permanent control" over Greenland's security. Denmark said the deal is "great for NATO and Europe." US President Donald Trump on Friday said that the US had reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland giving Washington permanent military access to the Arctic island. The Danish and Greenlandic governments also announced a breakthrough in negotiations, but stressed that the agreement respected Danish sovereignty over Greenland and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination. The agreement is expected to be signed next week on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Trump said the deal would allow the United States to maintain a permanent security presence in Greenland. "At my direction, we worked with representatives of Denmark and Greenland to guarantee that the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America," Trump wrote on Truth Social. A US State Department official said the agreement gave Washington permanent access, basing and overflight rights and would prevent China and Russia from establishing military bases on the island. Trump said the US would "immediately" begin expanding its military presence in Greenland. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Copenhagen emphasized a different aspect of the agreement, stressing that it did not alter Greenland's constitutional status. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement recognized "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom" as well as "the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination." "I am pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," Frederiksen said, calling it "great for NATO and Europe." Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen also welcomed the breakthrough. "It is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States, and the Western alliance," Nielsen said. He added that the agreement recognized "Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation." Since returning to the White House last year, Trump has pressed Denmark to sell Greenland to the United States and even threatened to take it by force, insisting that the island is crucial for US security. Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly stated that the island is not for sale and have condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there. passages: COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement on Tuesday aimed at ending months of tension over the Danish self-governing territory after US President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to take control of the vast Arctic island.
The agreement expresses support for a stronger NATO presence in the Arctic, and Denmark commits to further strengthen its own security posture in the region.
The deal bars investors from outside NATO member states, NATO partners or the European Union from having control or major influence over sensitive sectors in Greenland.

extraction.body: COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement on Tuesday aimed at ending months of tension over the Danish self-governing territory after US President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to take control of the vast Arctic island. Here are some key components of the deal, which adds to a 1951 US-Danish pact on Greenland’s defence, according to a text published by the Danish government. The agreement allows the United States to establish two new military bases — one at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and the other at Mestersvig on the east coast — and to expand Pituffik Space Base, currently its only active base on the island. US craft including planes and vessels get flyover, landing and undersea rights in all of Greenland, including territorial waters. The agreement does not specify troop numbers or timelines. The agreement expresses support for a stronger NATO presence in the Arctic, and Denmark commits to further strengthen its own security posture in the region. If Greenland ever become independent, Denmark and Greenland must ensure the new state remains in NATO, applying for membership if necessary. Non-NATO members are barred from having an ongoing military presence in Greenland. The agreement says it respects Greenland’s right to self-determination. Under the accord, the US must act in a way that respects Greenlandic society and the Greenlandic way of life. The agreement does not address US interests or investments into Greenland’s mining and resources sector. The deal bars investors from outside NATO member states, NATO partners or the European Union from having control or major influence over sensitive sectors in Greenland. Greenland will screen investments to enforce those rules. The parliaments of Greenland and Denmark must approve the agreement before it goes into effect. The pact has no end date and can be amended only by mutual consent. (Reporting by Louise Rasmussen and Stine Jacobsen; Editing by Cynthia Osterman) COPENAGHEN, 22 settembre (Reuters) - Martedì gli Stati Uniti, la Danimarca e la Groenlandia hanno firmato un accordo di sicurezza volto a porre fine a mesi di tensioni sul territorio danese autonomo, dopo le ripetute minacce del presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump di assumere il controllo della vasta isola artica. Ecco alcuni punti chiave dell’accordo, che va ad integrare un patto del 1951 tra Stati Uniti e Danimarca sulla difesa della Groenlandia, secondo un testo pubblicato dal governo danese. sources.title: Explainer-What is in the US-Greenland-Denmark security deal? - Internazionale
passages: COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement on Tuesday aimed at ending months of tension over the Danish self-governing territory after US President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to take control of the vast Arctic island.
The agreement expresses support for a stronger NATO presence in the Arctic, and Denmark commits to further strengthen its own security posture in the region.
The deal bars investors from outside NATO member states, NATO partners or the European Union from having control or major influence over sensitive sectors in Greenland.

The deal bars investors from outside NATO member states, NATO partners or the European Union from having control or major influence over sensitive sectors in Greenland.

extraction.body: COPENHAGEN, Sept 22 (Reuters) - The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a security agreement on Tuesday aimed at ending months of tension over the Danish self-governing territory after US President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to take control of the vast Arctic island. Here are some key components of the deal, which adds to a 1951 US-Danish pact on Greenland’s defence, according to a text published by the Danish government. The agreement allows the United States to establish two new military bases — one at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and the other at Mestersvig on the east coast — and to expand Pituffik Space Base, currently its only active base on the island. US craft including planes and vessels get flyover, landing and undersea rights in all of Greenland, including territorial waters. The agreement does not specify troop numbers or timelines. The agreement expresses support for a stronger NATO presence in the Arctic, and Denmark commits to further strengthen its own security posture in the region. If Greenland ever become independent, Denmark and Greenland must ensure the new state remains in NATO, applying for membership if necessary. Non-NATO members are barred from having an ongoing military presence in Greenland. The agreement says it respects Greenland’s right to self-determination. Under the accord, the US must act in a way that respects Greenlandic society and the Greenlandic way of life. The agreement does not address US interests or investments into Greenland’s mining and resources sector. The deal bars investors from outside NATO member states, NATO partners or the European Union from having control or major influence over sensitive sectors in Greenland. Greenland will screen investments to enforce those rules. The parliaments of Greenland and Denmark must approve the agreement before it goes into effect. The pact has no end date and can be amended only by mutual consent. (Reporting by Louise Rasmussen and Stine Jacobsen; Editing by Cynthia Osterman) COPENAGHEN, 22 settembre (Reuters) - Martedì gli Stati Uniti, la Danimarca e la Groenlandia hanno firmato un accordo di sicurezza volto a porre fine a mesi di tensioni sul territorio danese autonomo, dopo le ripetute minacce del presidente degli Stati Uniti Donald Trump di assumere il controllo della vasta isola artica. Ecco alcuni punti chiave dell’accordo, che va ad integrare un patto del 1951 tra Stati Uniti e Danimarca sulla difesa della Groenlandia, secondo un testo pubblicato dal governo danese. "We will be careful," Trump said in a Truth Social post. Trump's mention of the DOJ as a backstop came as he again downplayed potential dangers from AI , which he has repeatedly called a hoax in the past two weeks, after Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher at Anthropic , quit his job and warned that that company and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives" with the technology. The president has touted AI development by American companies as a competitive advantage for the United States, which he wants to maintain. "Whoever wins AI, WINS!" Trump wrote in his post. "We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I'm going to keep it that way!" he wrote. "I'm not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself." "We will be careful, and that's why we have the Department of Justice, and other Law Enforcement bodies, that will rein things in if we have to, but I will only encourage AI or, SI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)!" Trump wrote. The president, in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post, wrote, "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies." Since Coxon's warning, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind, have called for a slowdown of AI development and extra federal oversight of their industry. The White House has largely taken a light approach to AI regulation, with Trump's executive order in June laying out a loose plan for review. That order asked companies to voluntarily work with the administration to evaluate "covered frontier models" and give the government access up to 30 days before a broad release. passages: "We will be careful, and that's why we have the Department of Justice, and other Law Enforcement bodies, that will rein things in if we have to," Trump wrote on Truth Social on Monday.
President Donald Trump suggested there are existing ways to "rein" in AI.
In the US, states including California and Illinois have led AI regulation efforts as Congress has struggled to reach consensus.
Trump has issued multiple AI-related executive actions, but there are limits to what he can do.
One potential regulatory area could center around liability.
Earlier Monday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration would not grant frontier AI labs protection from such risks.
Trump and his administration are being closely watched to see how they respond to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's renewed push for federal regulation.
After Amodei renewed his request, Trump and Vice President JD Vance both expressed skepticism that AI companies would ask the government to impose regulations that would slow parts of the industry.

In his post on Monday, Trump reiterated his view that the current conversation around AI safety is a "hoax" akin to his stated opinions on climate change, questions about his 2016 campaign's relationship with Russia, and the circumstances of his first impeachment.
Trump has repeatedly expressed a preference to use a light touch when it comes to AI regulation.
Previously, Trump suggested that the only guardrail the US needed was himself because he was smart enough to know how to manage the technology.

extraction.body: President Donald Trump said Monday that the Department of Justice and other U.S. law enforcement agencies will rein in risks associated with artificial intelligence "if we have to." "We will be careful," Trump said in a Truth Social post. Trump's mention of the DOJ as a backstop came as he again downplayed potential dangers from AI , which he has repeatedly called a hoax in the past two weeks, after Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher at Anthropic , quit his job and warned that that company and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives" with the technology. The president has touted AI development by American companies as a competitive advantage for the United States, which he wants to maintain. "Whoever wins AI, WINS!" Trump wrote in his post. "We are leading now over China, and everyone else, and I'm going to keep it that way!" he wrote. "I'm not going to stifle Growth, of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution, or the Internet, itself." "We will be careful, and that's why we have the Department of Justice, and other Law Enforcement bodies, that will rein things in if we have to, but I will only encourage AI or, SI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)!" Trump wrote. The president, in a Sept. 14 Truth Social post, wrote, "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies." Since Coxon's warning, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman , SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind, have called for a slowdown of AI development and extra federal oversight of their industry. The White House has largely taken a light approach to AI regulation, with Trump's executive order in June laying out a loose plan for review. That order asked companies to voluntarily work with the administration to evaluate "covered frontier models" and give the government access up to 30 days before a broad release. extraction.body: Washington DC: The Donald Trump administration on Tuesday defended its decision to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The Justice Department said that the media houses can be barred from the White House at the US President’s will. The department, in a court filing, argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," reported CNN. The filing further contended that Trump has the authority to restrict access to private sections of the White House to safeguard sensitive national security information. “At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote in its filing, as reported by CNN. “The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns,” it added. The Justice Department’s court filing came a day ahead of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. The petitioners, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, are demanding for the immediate restoration of their media access. Reasons For Banning These Media Outlets: The latest court filings also include letters sent to the three media organisations on Tuesday, outlining the reasons cited by the President for imposing the access ban. These letters cite several stories published by the banned media outlets. The letter addressed to CNN referred to the network’s report about Trump’s plans for a “top secret” bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom under construction, along with several of its reports on the Iran war. The letter to MS NOW slammed the media house for its coverage of the Iran war. As per a CNN report citing these letters, Politico’s entry was banned due to its reporting on Iran, the ballroom and Russia sanctions. About The Dispute: The dispute began last week when Trump barred journalists from the three outlets from entering the White House grounds. CNN, MS NOW and Politico filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to restore their access, arguing that the restrictions violate their First Amendment rights. At the same time, ABC, CBS, Fox News, and NBC suspended their pooled television coverage of Trump after the White House prevented CNN from carrying out its scheduled role as pool representative during his trip to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump's Clarification: Trump strongly defended the decision in multiple Truth Social posts, rejecting the allegations that the White House was attacking the free press. “The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump wrote. “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.” He described the coverage from the three outlets as “corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control,” and said it was “a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!” Trump also argued that the media organizations should not automatically receive access to the White House.

The Justice Department has urged a federal court to uphold President Trump's ban on CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, arguing White House access is not a public right. The United States Department of Justice has formally defended President Donald Trump's decision to ban three major news organizations from the White House, arguing in a late-night court filing that presidential access is a "privilege—not a right." The legal maneuver seeks to uphold the administration's revocation of press credentials for journalists from CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, citing severe national security concerns and alleged breaches of professional decorum. The filing, submitted to a federal court in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday evening, arrived just hours before an emergency hearing concerning the media outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. The news organizations are suing the Trump administration to immediately restore their White House access, characterizing the ban as a flagrant violation of their First Amendment rights. The escalating legal battle underscores the highly adversarial relationship between the White House and the press corps during Trump's presidency, raising fundamental questions about the government's authority to control public information and exclude critical voices from the seat of executive power. In its submission to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the Justice Department argued that the First Amendment does not grant journalists an unrestrained, independent right to access highly controlled government facilities. The DOJ maintained that the president possesses broad, discretionary authority to manage entry to restricted areas, including the Oval Office. "The White House is the home and workplace for the Nation's Commander-in-Chief," DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik wrote in the filing. "But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by publishing sensitive or classified information." The government asserted that it holds a compelling interest in enforcing these minimum standards and safeguarding classified material. The DOJ further claimed that the administration is legally permitted to control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas "even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons," a stark legal position that challenges established norms of press freedom. The DOJ's filing included copies of formal letters sent by the White House Press Office to the three networks on Tuesday, outlining the administration's specific grievances. The letters accused the outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security" and cited a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents that the White House deemed dangerous. For CNN, the administration flagged January reports detailing the construction of a top-secret bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom, alongside coverage concerning US military munitions shortages amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. MSNOW was criticized for its reporting on the Iran war and its coverage of internal White House leak investigations. Politico faced similar accusations regarding its articles on Russian sanctions and the diplomatic fallout from the Middle East conflict. The letters provided the news organizations with a strict deadline of 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, to formally contest the initial decision, warning that failure to respond would render the revocations permanent. The media outlets have strongly denied that their reporting compromised national security. Legal representatives for the networks argue that the cited articles relied on corroborated sources and standard journalistic practices, portraying the administration's national security claims as a pretext for punishing unfavorable coverage. The current controversy erupted on Friday when Trump announced the bans via a post on his Truth Social platform, declaring the move "effective immediately." He justified the decision by accusing the networks of reporting "fiction and lies" and suggested that other media organizations might face similar expulsions. Press freedom advocates have condemned the bans as a retaliatory tactic designed to chill independent journalism. Legal experts note that federal courts have historically sided with the press when the Trump administration previously attempted to revoke individual credentials, such as the high-profile disputes involving CNN's Jim Acosta and Brian Karem during his first term. In those instances, courts ruled that the administration could not arbitrarily revoke credentials without providing rigorous due process. However, the Justice Department is now attempting to establish a broader legal precedent, leaning heavily on the argument that the physical security of the White House supersedes general press access rights. The government explicitly argued that the bans were not retaliatory, claiming that the administration would have taken the same action regarding the classified leaks regardless of the outlets' broader editorial criticism of the president. The outcome of Wednesday's emergency hearing will carry significant implications for the functioning of the White House press corps. Without a traveling pool representative from CNN, the television network pool was left empty during the president's movements earlier in the week, disrupting the standard distribution of presidential activities to the broader public. As the legal proceedings advance, the confrontation highlights a critical constitutional tension. While the government insists on its right to control the physical perimeter of the executive branch, media organizations warn that allowing a president to unilaterally ban specific outlets based on their reporting fundamentally undermines the democratic principle of a free and unhindered press. extraction.body: The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns. The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access. The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege—not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing. It contends that the three news outlets had “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik. The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes, and citing a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.” The letters cite stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia. The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims. The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say. The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post, where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.” He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.” Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated. First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional. CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech. The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.” U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds. Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN. On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” ​let journalists from CNN, ⁠MS ​NOW and ​Politico back into the White ​House if ​a court rules ‌against ⁠his decision to ban the ​media ​outlets ⁠from the White ​House grounds. Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins: “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual. The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities. Pool coverage is when one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which includes outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool.

extraction.body: Washington DC: The Donald Trump administration on Tuesday defended its decision to bar journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The Justice Department said that the media houses can be barred from the White House at the US President’s will. The department, in a court filing, argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right," reported CNN. The filing further contended that Trump has the authority to restrict access to private sections of the White House to safeguard sensitive national security information. “At the very least, the Government may control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office, even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons,” the Justice Department wrote in its filing, as reported by CNN. “The President has found that Plaintiffs have engaged in a number of reporting incidents that have threatened national security. Such reporting directly raises national security concerns,” it added. The Justice Department’s court filing came a day ahead of an emergency hearing before federal judge Timothy Kelly in Washington, DC. The petitioners, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, are demanding for the immediate restoration of their media access. Reasons For Banning These Media Outlets: The latest court filings also include letters sent to the three media organisations on Tuesday, outlining the reasons cited by the President for imposing the access ban. These letters cite several stories published by the banned media outlets. The letter addressed to CNN referred to the network’s report about Trump’s plans for a “top secret” bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom under construction, along with several of its reports on the Iran war. The letter to MS NOW slammed the media house for its coverage of the Iran war. The Justice Department has urged a federal court to uphold President Trump's ban on CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, arguing White House access is not a public right. The United States Department of Justice has formally defended President Donald Trump's decision to ban three major news organizations from the White House, arguing in a late-night court filing that presidential access is a "privilege—not a right." The legal maneuver seeks to uphold the administration's revocation of press credentials for journalists from CNN, MSNOW, and Politico, citing severe national security concerns and alleged breaches of professional decorum. The filing, submitted to a federal court in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday evening, arrived just hours before an emergency hearing concerning the media outlets' request for a temporary restraining order. The news organizations are suing the Trump administration to immediately restore their White House access, characterizing the ban as a flagrant violation of their First Amendment rights. The escalating legal battle underscores the highly adversarial relationship between the White House and the press corps during Trump's presidency, raising fundamental questions about the government's authority to control public information and exclude critical voices from the seat of executive power. In its submission to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, the Justice Department argued that the First Amendment does not grant journalists an unrestrained, independent right to access highly controlled government facilities. The DOJ maintained that the president possesses broad, discretionary authority to manage entry to restricted areas, including the Oval Office. "The White House is the home and workplace for the Nation's Commander-in-Chief," DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik wrote in the filing. "But the President concluded that they have failed to maintain basic minimum standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by publishing sensitive or classified information." The government asserted that it holds a compelling interest in enforcing these minimum standards and safeguarding classified material. The DOJ further claimed that the administration is legally permitted to control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas "even for viewpoint-discriminatory reasons," a stark legal position that challenges established norms of press freedom. The DOJ's filing included copies of formal letters sent by the White House Press Office to the three networks on Tuesday, outlining the administration's specific grievances. The letters accused the outlets of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security" and cited a non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents that the White House deemed dangerous. For CNN, the administration flagged January reports detailing the construction of a top-secret bunker beneath the East Wing ballroom, alongside coverage concerning US military munitions shortages amid the ongoing conflict with Iran. MSNOW was criticized for its reporting on the Iran war and its coverage of internal White House leak investigations. Politico faced similar accusations regarding its articles on Russian sanctions and the diplomatic fallout from the Middle East conflict. The letters provided the news organizations with a strict deadline of 5:00 p.m. on Friday, September 25, to formally contest the initial decision, warning that failure to respond would render the revocations permanent. The media outlets have strongly denied that their reporting compromised national security. Legal representatives for the networks argue that the cited articles relied on corroborated sources and standard journalistic practices, portraying the administration's national security claims as a pretext for punishing unfavorable coverage. The current controversy erupted on Friday when Trump announced the bans via a post on his Truth Social platform, declaring the move "effective immediately." He justified the decision by accusing the networks of reporting "fiction and lies" and suggested that other media organizations might face similar expulsions. Press freedom advocates have condemned the bans as a retaliatory tactic designed to chill independent journalism. Legal experts note that federal courts have historically sided with the press when the Trump administration previously attempted to revoke individual credentials, such as the high-profile disputes involving CNN's Jim Acosta and Brian Karem during his first term. In those instances, courts ruled that the administration could not arbitrarily revoke credentials without providing rigorous due process. However, the Justice Department is now attempting to establish a broader legal precedent, leaning heavily on the argument that the physical security of the White House supersedes general press access rights. The government explicitly argued that the bans were not retaliatory, claiming that the administration would have taken the same action regarding the classified leaks regardless of the outlets' broader editorial criticism of the president. The outcome of Wednesday's emergency hearing will carry significant implications for the functioning of the White House press corps. Without a traveling pool representative from CNN, the television network pool was left empty during the president's movements earlier in the week, disrupting the standard distribution of presidential activities to the broader public. As the legal proceedings advance, the confrontation highlights a critical constitutional tension. While the government insists on its right to control the physical perimeter of the executive branch, media organizations warn that allowing a president to unilaterally ban specific outlets based on their reporting fundamentally undermines the democratic principle of a free and unhindered press. extraction.body: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday told the UN General Assembly that the United States would change its official terminology for artificial intelligence (AI), saying the technology would now be referred to as “super intelligence”. He also firmly rejected calls for international supervision of artificial intelligence, calling them a "globalist scheme" to control the new technology. The announcement comes days after Trump said his administration would create an “AI Force” and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar, as Washington faces growing debate over the opportunities and risks associated with rapidly advancing AI systems. AI has also emerged as a major arena of competition between the US and China, with both countries seeking an advantage in advanced technologies. The issue is expected to feature in discussions when Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping next week. Trump also said his administration would rely on the existing criminal and civil justice system to deal with people who misuse AI. At the same time, he repeated his view that warnings and criticism about the potential dangers of AI amount to a “hoax”. Those concerns have intensified in recent weeks, with current and former AI researchers warning about the possibility of increasingly capable systems posing serious risks to humanity. One researcher has estimated that there is a greater than 10% chance of AI “killing all humans”. The terminology used by Trump also overlaps with a concept already being pursued by leading AI companies. Major firms have been racing to develop increasingly capable systems, with “super intelligence” generally referring to theoretical AI systems that would surpass human intellectual capabilities. Companies including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, which develop Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini respectively, have also disclosed security breaches and incidents involving the use of their AI systems for malicious activities. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development and advocated industry-wide measures including greater regulation and independent monitoring of AI model development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI founder Elon Musk have both expressed support for his recommendations. Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told the BBC that the industry may eventually need mandatory “kill switch” mechanisms that can be independently checked by third parties. The growing warnings have also pushed AI regulation higher on the US political agenda, with lawmakers proposing legislation aimed at addressing potential risks associated with the technology. Altman, however, said this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the rapid development of AI and the challenges involved in regulating it. He also argued that people should place greater trust in AI companies to ensure the technology is developed safely. He also firmly rejected calls for international supervision of artificial intelligence, calling them a "globalist scheme" to control the new technology. The announcement comes days after Trump said his administration would create an “AI Force” and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar, as Washington faces growing debate over the opportunities and risks associated with rapidly advancing AI systems. AI has also emerged as a major arena of competition between the US and China, with both countries seeking an advantage in advanced technologies. The issue is expected to feature in discussions when Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping next week. Trump also said his administration would rely on the existing criminal and civil justice system to deal with people who misuse AI. At the same time, he repeated his view that warnings and criticism about the potential dangers of AI amount to a “hoax”. Those concerns have intensified in recent weeks, with current and former AI researchers warning about the possibility of increasingly capable systems posing serious risks to humanity. One researcher has estimated that there is a greater than 10% chance of AI “killing all humans”. The terminology used by Trump also overlaps with a concept already being pursued by leading AI companies. Major firms have been racing to develop increasingly capable systems, with “super intelligence” generally referring to theoretical AI systems that would surpass human intellectual capabilities. Companies including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, which develop Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini respectively, have also disclosed security breaches and incidents involving the use of their AI systems for malicious activities. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown in AI development and advocated industry-wide measures including greater regulation and independent monitoring of AI model development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI founder Elon Musk have both expressed support for his recommendations. Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, told the BBC that the industry may eventually need mandatory “kill switch” mechanisms that can be independently checked by third parties. The growing warnings have also pushed AI regulation higher on the US political agenda, with lawmakers proposing legislation aimed at addressing potential risks associated with the technology. Altman, however, said this week that Washington has struggled to keep pace with the rapid development of AI and the challenges involved in regulating it. He also argued that people should place greater trust in AI companies to ensure the technology is developed safely. President Donald Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that the United States would change the name of artificial intelligence to “super intelligence” in government documents, arguing that “artificial” makes intelligence sound fake. Trump said, “From this point forward, all of United States documents and hopefully the world’s will be changed to use the much more accurate term super as opposed to artificial,” and he framed the move as a rejection of “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now.” “ From this point forward, all of the United States documents, and hopefully the world’s, will be changed to use the much more accurate term, super as opposed to artificial. ” Trump also said the U.S. would “only encourage super intelligence” and would “watch it closely through the Department of Justice,” while he asserted, “We’re leading now over China by a lot.” Trump compared the fears around AI to earlier warnings about global warming, saying “the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming” were now saying “AI is going to kill us all.” Trump allegedly uses Truth Social polls to choose the wording . Reported by The New Republic and Gizmodo . The Independent reported uncertainty about whether a formal implementation order existed, and the reporting reviewed at publication time found no confirmed binding federal directive implementing the terminology change. The Hill described Trump’s remarks as a renaming in “all U.S. documents,” while Trump told the UN that “The use of the word artificial makes intelligence sound fake,” and he added, “It is not fake. passages: State and federal regulators are rushing to fill the void in U.S. cryptocurrency regulation after the Clarity Act , a comprehensive set of proposed rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate .
The agency issued an order creating a temporary pathway for trading certain tokenized stocks, inching financial markets closer to 24/7 trading.
When asked how the agency plans to regulate crypto, the CFTC pointed CNBC to Chair Michael Selig's Sept.

16 statement where he said, "President Trump promised to deliver a future-proof crypto asset regulatory market structure one way or the other, and we will help him get the job done using our existing statutory authorities." CNBC also reached out to the SEC regarding next steps for regulating the digital asset industry, and a spokesperson said the agency will consider a proposal to "modernize the rules around custody of investment adviser client assets and fund assets, including to address crypto assets."

extraction.body: State and federal regulators are rushing to fill the void in U.S. cryptocurrency regulation after the Clarity Act , a comprehensive set of proposed rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate . Just two days after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, the Securities and Exchange Commission expanded its crypto rulebook under its existing authority. The agency issued an order creating a temporary pathway for trading certain tokenized stocks, inching financial markets closer to 24/7 trading. The same day, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission submitted a crypto rulemaking proposal to the White House for review. The details of the proposal weren't made public, but a post by the Office of Management and Budget confirmed the rules were pending review. The crypto industry , which had supported the Clarity Act, says it is eager for regulatory guidelines for the developing industry, as it has worked to shape the regulatory environment to its liking. "When you're thinking about traditional finance entering in and using some of this technology, they're being held back right now because there is this regulatory uncertainty," Summer Mersinger , CEO of the Blockchain Association and a former CFTC commissioner, said. "Having the regulators provide some sort of certainty is going to really open up the industry to more investment, more integration into traditional finance, and really grow the sector." And Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, who is a key industry player urging Congress to act on the Clarity Act, told CNBC after a failed Senate procedural vote on Sept. 15: "At this point, I don't think we can wait on Congress and the Senate." Senate banking committee Chairman Tim Scott , R-S.C., also called on federal agencies to set "clear rules of the road" for digital assets until Congress legislates. But new rules from federal agencies don't come quickly. When asked how the agency plans to regulate crypto, the CFTC pointed CNBC to Chair Michael Selig's Sept. 16 statement where he said, "President Trump promised to deliver a future-proof crypto asset regulatory market structure one way or the other, and we will help him get the job done using our existing statutory authorities." CNBC also reached out to the SEC regarding next steps for regulating the digital asset industry, and a spokesperson said the agency will consider a proposal to "modernize the rules around custody of investment adviser client assets and fund assets, including to address crypto assets." Caroline Pham , who served as acting CFTC chair from the day President Donald Trump took office for his second term until December, told CNBC that "a plan B to move forward at the agency level was always in the cards." Pham is now the CEO of MoonPay Institutional and chief legal officer and chief administrative officer for MoonPay , a crypto services provider. "You have to have a contingency plan," she said, explaining that the CFTC and SEC took that into account with the work the agencies have been doing since Trump's second term began. That includes the " Project Crypto " initiative introduced in July 2025 to modernize securities regulations and align the SEC and CFTC's crypto rules. In August 2025, Pham announced the CFTC would start implementing the recommendations from the President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets . As Washington grapples with crypto regulation, states are also fighting for the chance to regulate the asset class. In a Sept. 14 letter , a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general urged the Senate Banking Committee to oppose the Clarity Act, arguing the bill displaces states' abilities to regulate securities markets. "We write to urge the Senate to expressly preserve the police powers of the states and ensure that the states remain armed with the tools necessary to protect the American people from predatory scammers," they wrote to Scott and the panel's top Democrat Sen. Elizabeth Warren , of Massachusetts. Aaron Klein, senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, told CNBC he doesn't think states are best positioned to regulate national and international capital markets. "Capital market regulation, I think, needs to be done at the federal level," Klein , who was previously a top staff member for the Senate banking committee, said. "In terms of stopping fraud and scams, states have a lot of authority." He said that in the absence of a federal framework for crypto, states should be more aggressively monitoring payment processing and prosecuting criminals. Mersinger noted that state enforcement comes after a crime is already committed. "What we really need is the oversight from the federal side to make sure that we're not having these situations where [a] state AG has to come in and file a lawsuit because there was some bad actor involved or some of their constituents in their state were somehow harmed," she said. The midterm election is now taking center stage, but lawmakers haven't completely abandoned the Clarity Act. Sen. Thom Tillis , R-N.C., revised his vote to oppose the bill, allowing him to bring a motion to reconsider the legislation in the Senate. — CNBC's Tanaya Macheel and Garrett Downs contributed to this report. extraction.body: The CLARITY Act fell 11 votes short of Senate cloture on Sept. 15, shifting US crypto rulemaking to the SEC and CFTC, per Bernstein and StoneX analysts. Forty-nine US senators voted to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on Sept. 15, falling 11 short of the 60 needed to clear a cloture motion. The SEC had already begun laying groundwork before the vote. On Aug. 18, it proposed a framework for investment contracts involving crypto assets. That proposal includes exemptions for startups’ token issuances of up to $5 million over four years and for token issuers to raise up to $75 million over 12 months. SEC Chair Paul Atkins told CNBC on July 27 that the agency was "ready, willing, and able to come out with rules" if the Senate did not act. StoneX Financial analysts, led by Mark Palmer, described the bill as dead for this Congress. They cited just 14 working days remaining in the Senate before campaign season begins. Senator Cynthia Lummis said the next realistic window for the CLARITY Act may not open until 2030. Polymarket odds of the bill becoming law in 2026 had fallen from 82% in February to 16% ahead of the vote. StoneX also flagged a potential legal dispute over stablecoin rewards. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation have each proposed rules that could treat a stablecoin issuer as violating the GENIUS Act's yield ban. The concern centers on issuers paying affiliates that then pass rewards to stablecoin holders. StoneX analysts said this conflict could reach the courts after the GENIUS Act takes effect in January 2027. Bernstein said the CLARITY Act would have "fool-proofed the industry against political regime shifts" had it passed. With legislation off the table, the SEC and CFTC will now determine the shape of US crypto regulation through their own rulemaking authority. I'm a crypto writer and an environmental scientist.

"Having the regulators provide some sort of certainty is going to really open up the industry to more investment, more integration into traditional finance, and really grow the sector." And Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, who is a key industry player urging Congress to act on the Clarity Act, told CNBC after a failed Senate procedural vote on Sept. 15: "At this point, I don't think we can wait on Congress and the Senate." Senate banking committee Chairman Tim Scott , R-S.C., also called on federal agencies to set "clear rules of the road" for digital assets until Congress legislates. But new rules from federal agencies don't come quickly. When asked how the agency plans to regulate crypto, the CFTC pointed CNBC to Chair Michael Selig's Sept. 16 statement where he said, "President Trump promised to deliver a future-proof crypto asset regulatory market structure one way or the other, and we will help him get the job done using our existing statutory authorities." CNBC also reached out to the SEC regarding next steps for regulating the digital asset industry, and a spokesperson said the agency will consider a proposal to "modernize the rules around custody of investment adviser client assets and fund assets, including to address crypto assets." Caroline Pham , who served as acting CFTC chair from the day President Donald Trump took office for his second term until December, told CNBC that "a plan B to move forward at the agency level was always in the cards." Pham is now the CEO of MoonPay Institutional and chief legal officer and chief administrative officer for MoonPay , a crypto services provider. "You have to have a contingency plan," she said, explaining that the CFTC and SEC took that into account with the work the agencies have been doing since Trump's second term began. That includes the " Project Crypto " initiative introduced in July 2025 to modernize securities regulations and align the SEC and CFTC's crypto rules. In August 2025, Pham announced the CFTC would start implementing the recommendations from the President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets . As Washington grapples with crypto regulation, states are also fighting for the chance to regulate the asset class. In a Sept. 14 letter , a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general urged the Senate Banking Committee to oppose the Clarity Act, arguing the bill displaces states' abilities to regulate securities markets. "We write to urge the Senate to expressly preserve the police powers of the states and ensure that the states remain armed with the tools necessary to protect the American people from predatory scammers," they wrote to Scott and the panel's top Democrat Sen. Elizabeth Warren , of Massachusetts. Aaron Klein, senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, told CNBC he doesn't think states are best positioned to regulate national and international capital markets. "Capital market regulation, I think, needs to be done at the federal level," Klein , who was previously a top staff member for the Senate banking committee, said. "In terms of stopping fraud and scams, states have a lot of authority." He said that in the absence of a federal framework for crypto, states should be more aggressively monitoring payment processing and prosecuting criminals. Mersinger noted that state enforcement comes after a crime is already committed. "What we really need is the oversight from the federal side to make sure that we're not having these situations where [a] state AG has to come in and file a lawsuit because there was some bad actor involved or some of their constituents in their state were somehow harmed," she said. The midterm election is now taking center stage, but lawmakers haven't completely abandoned the Clarity Act. Sen. Thom Tillis , R-N.C., revised his vote to oppose the bill, allowing him to bring a motion to reconsider the legislation in the Senate. — CNBC's Tanaya Macheel and Garrett Downs contributed to this report. extraction.body: The CLARITY Act fell 11 votes short of Senate cloture on Sept. 15, shifting US crypto rulemaking to the SEC and CFTC, per Bernstein and StoneX analysts. Forty-nine US senators voted to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act on Sept. 15, falling 11 short of the 60 needed to clear a cloture motion. The SEC had already begun laying groundwork before the vote. On Aug. 18, it proposed a framework for investment contracts involving crypto assets. That proposal includes exemptions for startups’ token issuances of up to $5 million over four years and for token issuers to raise up to $75 million over 12 months. SEC Chair Paul Atkins told CNBC on July 27 that the agency was "ready, willing, and able to come out with rules" if the Senate did not act. StoneX Financial analysts, led by Mark Palmer, described the bill as dead for this Congress. They cited just 14 working days remaining in the Senate before campaign season begins. Senator Cynthia Lummis said the next realistic window for the CLARITY Act may not open until 2030. Polymarket odds of the bill becoming law in 2026 had fallen from 82% in February to 16% ahead of the vote. StoneX also flagged a potential legal dispute over stablecoin rewards. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation have each proposed rules that could treat a stablecoin issuer as violating the GENIUS Act's yield ban. The concern centers on issuers paying affiliates that then pass rewards to stablecoin holders. StoneX analysts said this conflict could reach the courts after the GENIUS Act takes effect in January 2027. Bernstein said the CLARITY Act would have "fool-proofed the industry against political regime shifts" had it passed. With legislation off the table, the SEC and CFTC will now determine the shape of US crypto regulation through their own rulemaking authority. I'm a crypto writer and an environmental scientist.

sources.title: Coinbase Launches Fixed-Rate USDC Loans Backed by Bitcoin Through Morpho Midnight: how 13 outlets framed it - NewsCord
passages: Coinbase rolled out fixed-rate, bitcoin-backed USDC loans that let users borrow the USDC stablecoin against their bitcoin with an interest rate and repayment date set at origination.
Coinbase positioned the new product as an alternative to its floating-rate lending, with Morpho Blue loans that have more than $1.4 billion in active loans backed by nearly $3 billion in collateral.

Coinbase’s fixed-rate loans arrived as other crypto lending and infrastructure integrations expanded, with CoinMarketCap describing Morpho’s 3.5 percentage point surge over the past 22 hours as tied to Coinbase and Circle integrations.

CoinMarketCap further said Circle launched Digital Asset-Backed Borrowing (DABB) using Morpho as the first supported lending protocol, with eligible institutional Circle Mint users depositing BTC, minting wrapped cirBTC, and borrowing USDC through a Morpho lending market on Arc and Ethereum.
Coinbase’s product uses Morpho Midnight on Base, while Coinbase’s existing variable-rate borrowing uses Morpho Blue, where rates change based on demand and supply conditions.

Morpho co-founder and CEO Paul Frambot said, “We’re now building on that foundation and starting to scale: new loan types and use cases, bringing onchain credit one step closer to the scale and diversity of global credit markets,” as Coinbase expanded its onchain borrowing options.

The announcement also tied the move to the bitcoin-backed credit market, which it said is currently sized at roughly $16 billion, according to the Bitcoin Digital Credit Report compiled by Apyx and BitcoinTreasuries.net.
9 of 11 outlets skipped it: midnight currently holds about $30m in deposits during rollout .

Coinbase rolled out fixed-rate, bitcoin-backed USDC loans that let users borrow the USDC stablecoin against their bitcoin with an interest rate and repayment date set at origination. Coinbase said the fixed-rate offering runs on Morpho Midnight, a decentralized, non-custodial lending protocol for fixed-rate and fixed-term crypto loans launched in July, and it settles transactions on Coinbase’s Ethereum layer 2 network Base. Coinbase positioned the new product as an alternative to its floating-rate lending, with Morpho Blue loans that have more than $1.4 billion in active loans backed by nearly $3 billion in collateral. Morpho co-founder and CEO Paul Frambot said, “We’re now building on that foundation and starting to scale: new loan types and use cases, bringing onchain credit one step closer to the scale and diversity of global credit markets,” as Coinbase expanded its onchain borrowing options. The announcement also tied the move to the bitcoin-backed credit market, which it said is currently sized at roughly $16 billion, according to the Bitcoin Digital Credit Report compiled by Apyx and BitcoinTreasuries.net. Coinbase set the terms at the time a loan is taken out, and it described the fixed-rate structure as giving users greater certainty over the cost and duration of borrowing. Coinbase’s product uses Morpho Midnight on Base, while Coinbase’s existing variable-rate borrowing uses Morpho Blue, where rates change based on demand and supply conditions. At its annual Snapdragon Summit, Qualcomm said that the new chips can aid in improved personalization for AI agents. The chips have new sensing hubs that can run small models of up to 200 million parameters. With the new sensing hub, smartphones can run a personal scribe locally and differentiate between speakers. Plus, it can build memory based on your usage for better suggestions for automating tasks. The company said that it can run a complete voice-in and voice-out agent through the new chip. The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 has a new accelerator element that’s designed to run models in a more efficient way. The high-end Extreme version can run a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model locally. This means that while the overall model size is 30B, the model only activates a certain number of parameters for a particular task. For comparison, at its Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) in June, Apple released a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model , the most advanced of its third generation of foundation models. The new Qualcomm CPU also provides pixel-level control for cameras to facilitate more pro-level experiences, along with improved stabilization and motion understanding. The Extreme version can support video recording at 8K 60fps and at 4K240 for ultra HD slow-motion. It also enables the new Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec for pro-level recording. What’s more, both chips can use AI to boost vocals and reduce noise. Plus, it has Qualcomm’s new voice bubble tech, which isolates users’ noise during calls. At the event, Motorola announced its Motorola Signature 27 smartphone, powered by the Snapdragon Gen 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with general availability sometime this year. Qualcomm has been working on more than 40 AI devices , but there is still a belief that a lot of people will use their phones for AI rather than other dedicated devices. Nothing co-founder Carl Pei has hinted at this trend in the past, and more recently, new Apple CEO John Ternus reinforced the same line of thought during the iPhone Duo launch earlier this month. extraction.body: Qualcomm today announced two flagship smartphone processors, called Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with a focus on facilitating better AI-focused features. At its annual Snapdragon Summit, Qualcomm said that the new chips can aid in improved personalization for AI agents. The chips have new sensing hubs that can run small models of up to 200 million parameters. With the new sensing hub, smartphones can run a personal scribe locally and differentiate between speakers. Plus, it can build memory based on your usage for better suggestions for automating tasks. The company said that it can run a complete voice-in and voice-out agent through the new chip. The Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 has a new accelerator element that’s designed to run models in a more efficient way. The high-end Extreme version can run a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model locally. This means that while the overall model size is 30B, the model only activates a certain number of parameters for a particular task. For comparison, at its Worldwide Developer Conference (WWDC) in June, Apple released a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model , the most advanced of its third generation of foundation models. The new Qualcomm CPU also provides pixel-level control for cameras to facilitate more pro-level experiences, along with improved stabilization and motion understanding. The Extreme version can support video recording at 8K 60fps and at 4K240 for ultra HD slow-motion. It also enables the new Advanced Professional Video (APV) codec for pro-level recording. What’s more, both chips can use AI to boost vocals and reduce noise. Plus, it has Qualcomm’s new voice bubble tech, which isolates users’ noise during calls. At the event, Motorola announced its Motorola Signature 27 smartphone, powered by the Snapdragon Gen 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, with general availability sometime this year. Qualcomm has been working on more than 40 AI devices , but there is still a belief that a lot of people will use their phones for AI rather than other dedicated devices. Nothing co-founder Carl Pei has hinted at this trend in the past, and more recently, new Apple CEO John Ternus reinforced the same line of thought during the iPhone Duo launch earlier this month. extraction.body: Investors got a hopeful signal on Thursday that bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) may defy its historically weak September trend. The world's largest cryptocurrency jumped more than 5% on Thursday to rise above $81,000 as worries about a Federal Reserve rate hike eased and Treasury yields dropped. The question is whether the token can remain above these levels, given that bitcoin has historically posted negative returns in September in nine of the past 15 years. "It's important data, and we should respect it," Fundstrat head of digital assets Sean Farrell said. However, the strategist noted that the token has "bucked" this historical monthly trend over the past three years. "We haven't seen a negative September for years, and seasonality — it's a helpful data point, but it is not a foolproof system for trading these markets," he said. The token is coming off a strong August rally, prompting some strategists to suggest that the crypto bear market may be nearing a bottom if it hasn't already passed it. "The recent BTC price movement suggests that the crypto winter is close to being over," Noelle Acheson, author of "Crypto Is Macro Now," told Yahoo Finance. The token rallied 25% last month as the Treasury Department's recent intervention in the bond market and assistance to Japan helped lift the prices of gold and crypto assets. Some of those gains were given back as oil prices surged and hawkish comments from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh raised concerns about the Fed's upcoming September rate decision. On Thursday, Fed governor Christopher Waller hinted he would support keeping rates unchanged if inflation eases. "I could see crypto and broader equities mounting a rally post-FOMC that could take bitcoin to a higher level than today into late September, early October, " David Grider, head of liquid investments at Finality Capital, told Yahoo Finance. Grider said the move would be driven by either a surprise Fed rate hold or by yields falling sharply after the first rate hike. The risk of a market correction still holds, in which case bitcoin would also be sold off. But crypto analysts see such a move as short-term. "So long as the Treasury is willing to intervene in the yield curve, we believe, the bid on 'hard assets' such as bitcoin stays," Bernstein analyst Gautam Chhugani wrote in a recent note. Chhugani and his team called a bottom for bitcoin earlier this year and have placed a $150,000 year-end price target on the token. With the exception of 2018 and last year, the fourth quarter has proven bullish for bitcoin. The token is down roughly 7% year to date and roughly 35% below its all-time high of more than $126,000 reached in early October 2025. Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance. Read the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance

The world's largest cryptocurrency jumped more than 5% on Thursday to rise above $81,000 as worries about a Federal Reserve rate hike eased and Treasury yields dropped.
The question is whether the token can remain above these levels, given that bitcoin has historically posted negative returns in September in nine of the past 15 years.
